description: Our project, Mission Architect, is an interactive game where players design and launch their own space mission. It teaches how real engineers balance mass, power, data and cost, and it is inspired by real NASA missions. We want to make space science fun and easy to learn for everyone.
summary: Mission Architect is an interactive game where players design and launch a complete space mission. Players choose a mission (Earth climate watch, Moon ice hunter or Mars atmosphere), build a spacecraft, select science instruments, then pick a rocket, an orbit and a mission length. A live dashboard tracks budget, mass, power, data and time, so players see how one decision affects the rest. A simulation then launches the mission with random events, and a report explains why it succeeded or fell short. Players can play solo or in a team of up to four, with roles such as mission planner and spacecraft engineer. It addresses the challenge by making real space mission trade-offs easy to experience and learn.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
Players pick one of three missions: Earth climate watch, Moon ice hunter or Mars air sniffer. They design the spacecraft (bus, solar array, battery, antenna, computer, pointing system), choose instruments, a launch vehicle, an orbit and a mission length. A live dashboard tracks budget, mass, power, data and mission time. A pre-launch review checks that everything fits, then a simulation runs the mission with random events such as solar flares, power dips and antenna faults. Finally, the game gives a score and explains why the mission succeeded or fell short.

What benefits does it have?

  • Shows how decisions affect each other: a bigger instrument adds science but also mass, power, data and cost.
  • Works for beginners and advanced players, with three difficulty levels.
  • Team mode teaches collaboration: each player has a role and everyone must approve the launch.
  • Runs in any browser, including phones, with nothing to install.

What is the intended impact of the project?
It makes mission design easy to try for students and space fans. Players learn by experimenting, failing and trying again, and they come away understanding why real missions are hard and why there is rarely one perfect design.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no server needed. [Add any other tools you used, such as your code editor.] The game was written with help from Claude, an AI assistant.

How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?

  • It turns engineering trade-offs into a game, with scoring for science, budget efficiency and design margins.
  • Team roles create real negotiation: the mission planner, spacecraft engineer, science lead and comms and budget chief each have a different priority.
  • Beginner mode hides advanced parts and random events, so new players aren’t overwhelmed.
  • The post-mission report explains why something happened, not just whether it was right or wrong.
  • Future ideas: more missions, online multiplayer, a tutorial, and real NASA data for parts and orbits.
